Intel.onboarding: There was no room yet when Francis first came to me — there was just him, a whiteboard sketch of something called Eventide, and a level of confidence in a chip that didn't exist that I honestly hadn't seen since I was young enough to have that kind of confidence myself. I told him the timeline was impossible. He said, correctly, that I'd said that before about things that eventually shipped. Intel didn't join NewGen. Intel was the reason there was a NewGen to join.
Intel.quote: I've spent a career watching companies chase the next quarter and call it vision. When Francis put 'tech for the new generation' on that whiteboard, my honest first reaction was — okay, but who's going to build it, and will they still be humble about it in year three? Intel's job in this room isn't to be the loudest chip. It's to be the one every other division can trust without asking twice. Stay humble, work hard, delight the generation that hasn't been born yet. That's the whole pitch to me.
Intel.spearheadRemark: Every tile on this chip only works because the scheduling silicon underneath it never sleeps on the job — Hardware Thread Director is the reason the rest of NewGen gets to argue about optics and sound instead of about jitter.

Lightmatter.onboarding: Eventide was already real by the time Francis called me, which is rarer than people think — usually it's a deck. He had tiles that worked in isolation and no way to move data between them at the speed the rest of the chip demanded. That's a physics problem before it's a business problem, and he knew that, which is the only reason I took the meeting seriously. We were company number two for a reason — interconnect is always the first thing that breaks once you actually build something worth connecting.
Lightmatter.quote: Copper was always a compromise we'd forgotten was a compromise. Every year we keep shipping electrons through wire, we're taxing the next generation's compute budget for no physical reason anymore. When Francis says 'build for the new generation,' the first-principles version of that sentence, to me, is: don't hand them our bottlenecks. Give them light.
Lightmatter.spearheadRemark: Foveros 2.0 riding actual photons between tiles instead of electrons through copper — that's not a faster bus, that's a different physics budget for everything built on top of it.

Sony.onboarding: When Francis explained to me the six-primary thesis — capture to display, one language, no compromise in between — I will say, honestly, first I thought this is very ambitious for outside person to propose to Sony. But he had already brought Intel and Lightmatter to table, and interconnect problem, they had solved already. So the only question remaining for me was: can our sensor and our panel finally speak the same language as chip that carries them. I entered that room as third, and I remember thinking, this room already has more conviction in it than most companies have in fifty years.
Sony.quote: At Sony we have one word we return to for everything — Kando. Emotional impact. The new generation Francis speaks of, they will not remember spec sheet of sensor that captured their childhood. They will remember only how it felt to watch it back. My commitment to this table is simple: whatever silicon we build together, it must still make someone feel something, thirty years from now.
Sony.spearheadRemark: A hexa-stacked RGBMCY sensor talking directly to a six-primary panel over one link, with nothing in between that has to guess — that's the whole 'capture to glass' promise sitting in two pieces of Sony glass.

ASUS.onboarding: Francis didn't come to me asking for a material. He came to me with a CPU nobody had a chassis worthy of yet — the Xeon 9 599HKX — and a very specific, very stubborn demand: eighteen inches, dual screen, silent below eight watts, and a dock that lets the same chip hit two thousand watts with no compromise between the two states. I told him that was three or four different laptops pretending to be one. He said, correctly, that was exactly the point.
ASUS.quote: 'In Search of Incredible' was never a slogan to me, it was a standard nobody was allowed to lower. Francis didn't ask us to build a fast laptop. He asked us to build a laptop that is silent doing email and a full workstation the moment you dock it — and to not treat those as two different machines. We do not paint our chassis, we dope the crystal lattice, and now we've built one machine that has to be two things perfectly instead of one thing adequately. That is the incredible we were actually searching for.
ASUS.spearheadRemark: 0.5 watts to 2000 watts, on demand, out of the same silicon and the same chassis — that dynamic range is the whole argument for vertical integration made physical, in one machine you can actually close the lid on.
specBlock: 18-inch chassis, dual-screen ProArt DUO layout, engineered around a genuinely desktop-class CPU rather than a downclocked mobile part
0.5W–200W dynamic power envelope inside the chassis alone — full efficiency-core idle through sustained full-tilt Xeon 9 performance, slim form factor maintained throughout
Massive internal battery sized to actually matter at that power envelope, not a token cell

Magnetic wireless peripheral system — keyboard and trackpad detach and reattach magnetically, wireless from day one (Bluetooth couldn't hold the bandwidth a workstation laptop needed — this is the seed of the Hollyland collaboration)
Companion DOCK, sold/bundled as part of the system, unlocking the X9 599HKX's full 2000W ceiling with zero throttling
GaN SUPERVOOC mini fast charger — co-developed with OPPO's SUPERVOOC fast-charging division, the first laptop-class GaN SUPERVOOC charger ever shipped
Shimoda-collaboration carry case, purpose-fit for the laptop + dock + charger + peripherals as one traveling system
Ceraluminesium Sapphire chassis — the functionally-graded metal-ceramic detailed as a material choice within this laptop's design
Noctua-collaboration cooling for both the internal laptop thermal solution and the external dock — internal cooling genuinely fanless below 8W sustained load

OPPO.onboarding: By the time I was invited, the pipeline already worked in laboratory. Francis's question to me was not only 'can you make a networking tile.' He also asked, almost as afterthought, 'can your fast-charging team make something small enough to fit in a laptop bag but strong enough to matter.' I did not expect SUPERVOOC to end up inside an ASUS laptop dock. But this is, I think, exactly what NewGen is — nobody's technology stays in its own lane for long.
OPPO.quote: I do not think a company needs to be loud to have a mission. Benfen — knowing your role, and doing it without seeking credit. But I will say this clearly: OPPO's role in NewGen is not small. We are the reason a sensor with six primaries and a chip with a mind of its own becomes something a person actually holds, actually trusts — and now, something that charges a workstation laptop in a fraction of the time anyone expected. The phone is where the new generation first touches everything we built. That is not a small duty.
OPPO.spearheadRemark: The phone is the honest test of everything else on this page — if the six-primary pipeline doesn't survive being shrunk into something that fits in a pocket and gets dropped, none of the rest of it matters.

Ford.onboarding: Francis flew out and the first thing he asked me wasn't about horsepower, it was about dashboards — could a cabin display actually show six real primaries instead of faking two of them. By then he already had chip guys, glass guys, connection guys, laptop guys sitting at that table. I walked in a little late to the party, honestly, and the bar was already stupid high.
Ford.quote: Look, I've been a car guy since I was a kid named Jimmy Car-Car, so when somebody tells me we're building the dashboard for the next generation, I don't hear a spec sheet — I hear my own kids someday sitting in something we made and trusting it. We are maybe in the first inning of a nine-inning game on this vertical-integration thing, but I'd rather be honest about inning one than pretend we're already in extras.
Ford.spearheadRemark: A cabin display running the same six-primary pipeline as the sensor that shot the movie you're watching in the back seat — that's the platform leaving the desk and getting on the road.

BO.onboarding: I'll admit, my first honest reaction when Francis called was not excitement, it was a question: why does a company that has just spent an hour convincing Sony to hand over their sensor and their panel now also want my division, when Sony has audio engineers of their own. I asked him directly. He told me, plainly, that Sony builds toward the eye, and he needed someone who builds toward the ear the same way — with nothing borrowed, nothing shared with another product line internally. There was a moment of real tension in that room before I said yes, because I think everyone, including Sony's people, wanted to know whether two very different definitions of 'quality' could actually share a table without one of them quietly winning. I don't think either one 'won.' I think we just stopped pretending sound was a smaller problem than sight.
BO.quote: In Denmark we have a habit of saying less than we mean and building more than we promise. So when Francis asked what B&O owes the new generation, my answer is not a bigger speaker. It is a quieter room around a better one. Klangkerne only earns its name if a twenty-year-old somewhere trusts it the way their grandmother trusted a record player.
BO.spearheadRemark: Sound was the one sense nobody else at that table was building for on purpose — Klangkerne is what happens when you finally give the ear the same dedicated silicon the eye already had.

ShallXR.onboarding: By the time Francis contact our team, Play For Dream headset already exist, already very immersive for the eyes. But eyes is not whole body. He ask me, very simply: what happen to a person's stomach, their balance, their whole body, when the headset says you are falling but the chair says you are sitting still. Nobody at that table had good answer yet, because nobody had thought about body as separate problem from eyes. I say yes before he finish explaining, because I already know we solve this — this is exactly what iFly Chair is for.
ShallXR.quote: Our mission always is to bring people beyond boundary of what their body tells them is real — this is what 'go beyond reality' actually mean for us, not slogan, engineering target. A headset can show the fall. Only we can make the body believe the fall. We are the motion underneath Play For Dream's image — the part of immersion that lives below the neck.
ShallXR.spearheadRemark: The eyes can be fooled by a headset in isolation — the inner ear can't. ShallXR is the piece that keeps the illusion honest below the neck.

PlayForDream.onboarding:
I will say, first, I was confused. Francis tells me the display technology is CRT — and my honest first reaction is, CRT, this is what my father's generation threw away, why are we going backward. I have spent my whole career trying to escape the pixel grid, the fixed resolution, the flat-panel limitations, and here is someone telling me the answer was a scanning tube. I almost said no in that first meeting, I will admit this.

But then he explains it properly — not nostalgia, physics. Vector scan, no fixed pixel grid at all, which means foveation is not a software trick anymore, it is structural. The beam simply spends more time where the eye is actually looking. I have worked in this industry fifteen years and nobody, not one engineer, not one company, had said this sentence to me before. Sony had the display sitting on a bench, extremely beautiful, and — I think this is important to say — even Sony's own people had not fully connected what it meant for headset foveation the way Francis had. He was not the display engineer in that room. He was the one who understood what the display engineers had actually built, better than they did. I remember thinking, this man has never held a soldering iron in a display lab, and he just explained my industry's next ten years back to me. I said yes before I finished being embarrassed about almost saying no.
PlayForDream.quote: Everyone in this room is building one piece of pipeline. My job is to build the thing you put on your face and forget is hardware — and I will say honestly, I did not expect that thing to be built around a technology my own industry had already decided was finished. CRT was never the past that XR left behind. It was the future nobody in my industry looked back far enough to see, until Francis did. Give me Sony's panel, Intel's iDP link, and ShallXR's motion platform underneath me, and I give you a room nobody wants to take off.
PlayForDream.spearheadRemark: Vector scan means foveation stops being a software trick and becomes a property of the beam itself — that's not a headset feature, that's a different relationship between the eye and the display, and it was sitting in a warehouse the whole time.

Noctua.onboarding: Francis's team called about a dock, not a laptop — two thousand watts, they said, and it needs to be quiet enough to sit on a desk next to someone working. I've heard 'quiet and powerful' as a request for twenty years, usually meaning one or the other. Then he mentioned the laptop itself needed to run completely fanless under eight watts, which is a much harder and much more honest engineering problem than the loud one. We didn't get invited for the impressive number. We got invited for the number nobody else thought to ask about.
Noctua.quote: It's still the same annoyance with noisy environments that fuels our passion to make things quieter — that hasn't changed in twenty years, and it won't change because the chip inside got faster. So our part of this is simple: whatever Intel puts inside that chassis, whatever power the dock has to dissipate, the person sitting next to it should still be able to think in silence. Performance-to-noise efficiency isn't a spec category for us. It's the whole job.
Noctua.spearheadRemark: Nobody asks the fanless question until the silence stops being free — Noctua is the reason 0.5 watts and 2000 watts can share one chassis without either one being loud about it.

Hollyland.onboarding: We were invited twice, really, in the same conversation. First for the obvious reason — getting a six-primary camera signal off a set wirelessly without losing a channel. But then Francis mentioned, almost as a side note, that ASUS's new laptop had a magnetic wireless keyboard that Bluetooth simply couldn't keep up with, and did we have anything that could. It's been a tough road getting our transmission gear taken seriously at all, so having two completely different problems solved by the same underlying idea meant a lot.
Hollyland.quote: It has not been an easy road getting our transmission gear to where creators actually trust it, so I want to say first — thank you to everyone at this table for letting a smaller company carry something as important as the signal, twice over now. A six-primary sensor means nothing if the link drops, and neither does a beautiful magnetic keyboard if it lags behind your typing. Our job for the new generation is the most invisible one here, on set and now on the desk, and I am proud of both.
Hollyland.spearheadRemark: The same low-latency instinct that keeps a six-primary signal alive across a film set is the instinct that keeps a keyboard from ever feeling wireless — that's one company solving the same problem twice, in two rooms nobody expected to be the same room.

Shimoda.onboarding:
I've had a lot of pitch meetings in my time, and usually I can tell within two minutes what someone actually wants from Shimoda — a logo on a product page, a discount code, a co-branding favor. Francis was not that. He didn't open with a spec sheet or a deadline like I gather he does with everyone else. He opened by telling me about a Urban Explore 30 he'd carried through Italy and then through Japan as a kid, a Sony body and a 70-200 f/2.8 GM II stuffed inside it, and how the bag never once made him think about the bag on a hike he clearly still thinks about all the time. I make gear for people exactly like that, so I'll admit, he had me before he'd said a word about NewGen.

Then he shifted, and this is the part I actually remember most — he leaned forward and said, more or less, 'every other company at this table is building something that can break. You're the only one whose entire job is making sure none of it does. You are the company who protects all of it.' I don't think anyone had ever put it to me that plainly before. Camera bag makers don't usually get told we're the last line of defense for a six-primary sensor or a Xeon-class laptop — we get told we're an accessory. He wasn't pitching me an accessory. He was telling me, with a straight face and real conviction, that Shimoda was the reason any of the rest of it would survive contact with a person's actual life. I've built this whole company around not letting a hike be ruined by carrying a camera properly. Somehow this stranger understood that better, and faster, than most of my own team did in our first year.
Shimoda.quote: I'll be honest, I'm not sure I belong in a room with this much silicon talk — my whole design philosophy came from being annoyed that I had to choose between a good hike and carrying my camera gear properly. But that's exactly the new-generation problem, isn't it? Nobody should have to compromise the actual living of their life to carry the tools NewGen builds. My job is the last unglamorous layer: the bag has to survive the climb, or none of the six primaries in the world matter. And for what it's worth — hearing that a kid once carried an Urban Explore up an Italian hillside with a long lens in it and never once thought about the bag failing him? That's the only review that's ever actually mattered to me.
Shimoda.spearheadRemark: Every watt, every primary, every micron of dopant chemistry on this page is worth exactly nothing if it doesn't survive the trailhead — Shimoda is the last layer, and it's the one I actually lost sleep over before I found them.
